subject: feminism
title: Wages for Housework: the 1970s campaign to treat unpaid domestic labor as work
dek: In 1972 a group of feminists in Padua, London, and New York began to argue that housework is work that capitalism depends on and does not pay for. This lesson explains that argument first, then follows the campaign from Padua to New York, the pamphlet Wages Against Housework, the criticism it drew from other feminists, and its return in debates about care work and social reproduction.
honesty: This lesson describes Wages for Housework as a specific campaign with dated groups, texts, and arguments. Feminists disagreed sharply about it then and still do, so the lesson presents the criticism next to the claims. Quotations from Federici come from her 1975 pamphlet. Dates for the smaller groups, including Wages Due Lesbians, are given only as precisely as the sources allow.

timeline.label: Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto
timeline.detail: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, analyzing capitalism and class struggle. Later Marxist feminists argued that Marx's analysis of labor left out the unwaged work of the household.

timeline.label: Marx: Capital, Volume 1
timeline.detail: Marx's Capital analyzes how workers sell their labor-power for wages and how capital depends on that labor-power being renewed every day and every generation. Wages for Housework writers asked who does the work of renewing it.

timeline.label: Betty Friedan: The Feminine Mystique
timeline.detail: Friedan's book describes the dissatisfaction of middle-class American housewives confined to domesticity and encourages women to enter paid work. Wages for Housework writers later argued that this left the unpaid work at home untouched.

timeline.label: Margaret Benston: 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation'
timeline.detail: Benston argues that women's unpaid household work is a form of production on which the economy relies, an early statement of an argument that fed into the domestic labour debate of the 1970s.

timeline.label: The domestic labour debate
timeline.detail: Marxist feminists, including Wally Seccombe and Jean Gardiner, debate whether housework produces value in Marx's sense and whether a wage demand is strategically useful or reinforces women's domestic role.

timeline.label: Manchester conference and the International Feminist Collective
timeline.detail: In March, Selma James presents 'Women, the Unions and Work, or What Is Not to Be Done' in Manchester, listing wages for housework among her demands. In 1972 the International Feminist Collective is formed in Padua, Italy, to launch the campaign, with Dalla Costa, James, Federici, and Brigitte Galtier named as founders.

timeline.label: Dalla Costa and James: The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
timeline.detail: Falling Wall Press in Bristol publishes the pamphlet by Mariarosa Dalla Costa and Selma James, which argues that women's unpaid work in the home is part of capitalist production and starts the domestic labour debate.

timeline.label: New York Wages for Housework Committee distributes its first flyer
timeline.detail: The New York committee's first flyer is titled 'We Can't Afford to Work for Love.' Silvia Federici is among the organizers.

timeline.label: Italian groups take the name Salario al Lavoro Domestico
timeline.detail: Local groups campaigning for wages for housework appear in several Italian cities, including the Padua group around Dalla Costa.

timeline.label: Poster: 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!'
timeline.detail: The New York committee produces a poster drawn by Jacquie Ursula Caldwell, with text by Judy Quinlan of the Toronto committee, listing the tasks women want to be paid for.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Wages Against Housework
timeline.detail: The Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press publish Federici's pamphlet in April. Despite the title, it argues for the wage demand as a political perspective that makes housework visible so that it can be refused.

timeline.label: Black Women for Wages for Housework founded in New York
timeline.detail: Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown found the group, which focuses on the situation of Black and third-world women and calls for reparations for slavery, imperialism, and neo-colonialism.

timeline.label: Icelandic women's day off, 24 October
timeline.detail: About 90% of Icelandic women stay away from paid work and housework for a day. Iceland passes an equal-rights law the following year. The strike was not a Wages for Housework action, but it showed how much of daily life depends on women's work.

timeline.label: UN World Conference on Women, Mexico City
timeline.detail: The UN's first World Conference on Women, held from 19 June to 2 July as part of International Women's Year, adopts a World Plan of Action. Many delegates from developing countries regard sexism as a Western concern.

timeline.label: Wages Due Lesbians
timeline.detail: Wages Due Lesbians, one of three autonomous groups formed in the campaign between 1974 and 1976, wants lesbians included in the wage demand. Francie Wyland's 1976 pamphlet links child custody, motherhood, and lesbianism to the case for wages.

timeline.label: Houston conference and the end of the New York committee
timeline.detail: Black Women for Wages for Housework work with Beulah Sanders and Johnnie Tillmon of the National Welfare Rights Organization to get the Houston women's conference to agree that welfare payments should be called a wage. The New York committee dissolves in the same year, and the Padua group leaves the campaign and dissolves soon afterward.

timeline.label: Angela Davis: Women, Race & Class
timeline.detail: Davis's book analyzes the histories of Black and white women in the United States. Its housework chapter argues for socializing housework and for women's participation in wage labor, and is skeptical that a wage for housework would free women from the home.

timeline.label: Global Women's Strike, 8 March
timeline.detail: Women in more than 60 countries take part in the strike, called by the International Wages for Housework Campaign after a 1999 appeal from Irish women. It is coordinated from London and Selma James is one of its coordinators.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Caliban and the Witch
timeline.detail: Federici publishes a history of the witch hunts and the rise of capitalism, arguing that capitalism depended on disciplining women into unpaid reproductive work.

timeline.label: Social reproduction theory
timeline.detail: Tithi Bhattacharya, Nancy Fraser, Cinzia Arruzza, Susan Ferguson, and others develop social reproduction theory, which analyzes how capitalism depends on the unpaid and underpaid work of caring, cleaning, feeding, and raising the next generation.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Revolution at Point Zero
timeline.detail: Federici publishes a collection of her essays on housework, reproduction, and feminist struggle (PM Press), which brings her 1970s texts to a new readership.

timeline.label: China's civil code and a Beijing divorce ruling
timeline.detail: Article 1088 of China's new civil code lets a spouse who did more caregiving ask for compensation at divorce. A Beijing court orders a husband to pay his former wife 50,000 yuan for five years of housework.

read.title: Silvia Federici — Wages Against Housework (1975)
read.note: Federici's clearest statement. Despite the title, it argues for the wage demand as a political perspective that makes housework visible so that it can be refused, and it challenges the idea that women do housework out of love. This is a PDF of the full text.

read.title: Silvia Federici — Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation (Autonomedia, 2004)
read.note: Federici's major book extending the Wages for Housework analysis historically. Argues that the European witch-hunts, enclosures, and colonization were strategies to discipline women's bodies, control reproduction, and establish the unpaid domestic sphere that capitalism requires. Widely taught. Wikipedia entry.

read.title: Angela Davis — Women, Race & Class (Random House, 1981)
read.note: Davis's 1981 book traces the histories of Black and white women in the United States. Its housework chapter argues for socializing domestic labor and for women's participation in wage labor, and it is a useful counterweight to the wage demand.

read.title: Tithi Bhattacharya, ed. — Social Reproduction Theory: Remapping Class, Recentering Oppression (Pluto Press, 2017)
read.note: Contemporary collection reviving and refining the Wages for Housework analysis through social reproduction theory. Essays by Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, Susan Ferguson, and others analyze how capitalism depends on unwaged care work. Publisher page.

read.title: Leopoldina Fortunati — The Arcane of Reproduction: Housework, Prostitution, Labor and Capital (Autonomedia, 1995; original Italian 1981)
read.note: Fortunati, an Italian autonomist feminist, extends the Wages for Housework argument, analyzing prostitution alongside housework. Full text hosted on libcom.org.

read.title: Wikipedia — Wages for Housework
read.note: Open encyclopedia entry covering the campaign's history, key figures, arguments, criticisms, and legacy. Includes timeline and bibliography.

read.title: Wikipedia — 1975 Icelandic Women's Strike
read.note: Open entry on the 24 October 1975 women's day off in Iceland, when 90% of women stopped paid and unpaid work. Contextualizes Wages for Housework within contemporaneous direct action.

read.title: Wikipedia — Selma James
read.note: Biography of Selma James (born 1930), American-British feminist, co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the Power of Women Collective, and long-time organizer with the Global Women's Strike.

read.title: Wikipedia — Silvia Federici
read.note: Biography of Silvia Federici (born 1942), Italian-American scholar and activist, co-founder of the New York Wages for Housework Committee, author of Caliban and the Witch and Revolution at Point Zero.

read.title: Wikipedia — Mariarosa Dalla Costa
read.note: Biography of Mariarosa Dalla Costa (born 1943), Italian autonomist feminist, co-author of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community, member of Lotta Femminista, and co-founder of the International Feminist Collective.

fun_fact.title: The cover of Federici's pamphlet is a list of slogans
fun_fact.text: Wages Against Housework opens with a list of one-line replies that became famous: 'They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work. They call it frigidity. We call it absenteeism. Every miscarriage is a work accident.' And on smiles: 'More smiles? More money.' The title confuses new readers, because the campaign wanted wages. Federici explained that the demand was a way to make housework visible and refuse it, and that is why she put 'against' in the title.

glossary.explain: A feminist campaign launched in 1972 demanding that women be paid by the state for the work of cooking, cleaning, childcare, and other domestic labor—work that the campaign argued is essential to capitalist production but made invisible and unpaid.

The organization co-founded in Padua, Italy, in 1972 by Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici, and Brigitte Galtier to promote the Wages for Housework demand and analysis internationally.

Italian autonomist feminist (born 1943), member of Lotta Femminista, co-author with Selma James of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972), and co-founder of the International Feminist Collective.

American-British feminist activist and writer (born 1930), co-author of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972), co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the Power of Women Collective in London, and organizer of the Global Women's Strike from 2000.

Italian-American feminist scholar and activist (born 1942), co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the New York Wages for Housework Committee, author of Wages Against Housework (1975), Caliban and the Witch (2004), and Revolution at Point Zero (2012).
One of the four women named as founders of the International Wages for Housework Campaign in 1972, with Dalla Costa, James, and Federici.

glossary.term: The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
aliases: Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
glossary.explain: The 1972 pamphlet by Mariarosa Dalla Costa and Selma James, published by Falling Wall Press in Bristol. It argues that women's unpaid work in the home is part of capitalist production, and it started the domestic labour debate.

Silvia Federici's 1975 pamphlet, published jointly by the Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press (first edition April 1975). It presents the wage demand as a political perspective that makes housework visible so it can be refused.

The work of bearing, raising, feeding, clothing, cleaning, and caring for workers—reproducing labor-power on a daily and generational basis. Wages for Housework theorists argue this labor is essential to capitalism but unwaged and naturalized as women's duty.

In Marxist theory, labor that produces surplus value for capital. Classical Marxism treated only wage labor in commodity production as productive. Wages for Housework theorists argued that housework is productive because it produces labor-power, the commodity workers sell.

The capacity to work that workers sell to capitalists for a wage. Marx analyzed how capital buys labor-power and extracts surplus value. Wages for Housework theorists argued that housework produces and reproduces this capacity, making it productive labor capital refuses to pay for.

The 1970s Marxist feminist debate over whether housework produces value, whether it is productive or unproductive labor in Marx's technical sense, and whether the demand for wages is politically useful or a trap. Key contributors included Wally Seccombe, Jean Gardiner, and Heidi Hartmann.

Work done without a wage. Wages for Housework emphasized that housework is work—socially necessary labor—but capital's refusal to pay for it keeps it invisible and naturalized as love, duty, or women's nature.

glossary.term: New York Wages for Housework Committee
glossary.explain: New York group of the campaign, started by Silvia Federici and others. Its first flyer in 1973 was 'We Can't Afford to Work for Love'; it produced the 1974 poster 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!' and ran a campaign office in Brooklyn. It dissolved in 1977.

Group formed in London and Bristol by Selma James and a few other women after the 1972 Manchester women's liberation conference. It became the Wages for Housework Campaign in 1975 and co-published Federici's Wages Against Housework with Falling Wall Press.
The Toronto group of the Wages for Housework campaign. Judy Quinlan, a member, wrote 'Notice to All Governments,' the text of the 1974 poster 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!'

glossary.term: Black Women for Wages for Housework
glossary.explain: Autonomous group inside the Wages for Housework Campaign, founded in New York in 1975 by Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown. It focused on the situation of Black and third-world women, called for reparations for slavery, imperialism, and neo-colonialism, and in 1977 helped win agreement at the Houston women's conference that welfare payments should be called a wage.
Activist who co-founded Black Women for Wages for Housework in 1975 with Margaret Prescod.

Autonomous group inside the Wages for Housework Campaign, formed between 1974 and 1976 in Britain, the United States, and Canada. It wanted lesbians included in the wage demand and the extra work of surviving in a hostile and prejudiced society recognized as work.
Member of Wages Due Lesbians Toronto and author of an essay on child custody, motherhood, lesbianism, and the case for Wages for Housework, published as a pamphlet in 1976.

The work of cooking, cleaning, shopping, laundry, childcare, and other tasks required to maintain a household and reproduce labor-power. Wages for Housework argued this is work essential to capitalism but made invisible by being unwaged and naturalized as women's love or duty.

Italian feminist movement (the name means Feminist Struggle). Mariarosa Dalla Costa was a member. Lotta Femminista developed autonomist feminist analysis linking housework to capitalist exploitation and women's position to broader class struggle.

A strand of Marxist theory emerging in Italy in the 1960s–1970s emphasizing workers' autonomy and refusal of work as the motor of capitalist crisis. Wages for Housework theorists extended this analysis to unwaged domestic labor and women's refusal.

American political activist, scholar, and author (born 1944). In Women, Race & Class (1981) she analyzed the histories of Black and white women in the United States and argued for socializing housework and for women's participation in wage labor.
Angela Davis's 1981 book (Random House) on the histories of Black and white women in the United States, including the chapter on housework that argues for socializing domestic labor.

On 24 October 1975, approximately 90% of Icelandic women stopped paid work and refused housework and childcare for one day, demonstrating the indispensability of women's labor. Iceland passed an equal-rights law the following year.

The United Nations declared 1975 International Women's Year and held the first World Conference on Women in Mexico City from 19 June to 2 July 1975. It adopted a World Plan of Action and led to the UN Decade for Women.

Name by which the International Wages for Housework Campaign became widely known after the strike it called for 8 March 2000, in which women in more than 60 countries took part. It is coordinated from London, and Selma James is a coordinator.

aliases: Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation
glossary.explain: Silvia Federici's 2004 book (Autonomedia). Reinterprets the European witch-hunts, enclosures, and colonization as strategies to control women's bodies and reproduction, establishing the unpaid domestic sphere capitalism requires. Extends the Wages for Housework analysis historically.

A strand of Marxist feminist theory arguing that capitalism depends on the reproduction of labor-power—the daily and generational work of caring, feeding, cleaning, raising children—most of which is unwaged or underpaid. Revives and refines the Wages for Housework analysis in the 2010s. Key theorists include Tithi Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, Nancy Fraser.

In Marx's Capital, the historical process by which peasants were separated from land and turned into wage laborers—the violent origin of capitalism. Federici reinterprets witch-hunts and the creation of the unwaged domestic sphere as forms of primitive accumulation targeting women's bodies and labor.

The historical process of privatizing common land in Europe, forcing peasants off the land and into wage labor. Federici links enclosures to the disciplining of women and the creation of the domestic sphere as an unpaid zone of reproduction.

The labor of caring for dependents—children, elderly, sick, disabled. Contemporary feminist political economy debates how care work is distributed, who pays for it, and how its undervaluation structures gender, race, and class hierarchies. Wages for Housework prefigured these debates.

A policy proposal to give all citizens a regular, unconditional cash payment. Some feminists link basic income to the Wages for Housework demand, arguing it would recognize unwaged reproductive labor; others worry it could subsidize capital by keeping wages low.

Indian-American Marxist feminist scholar and organizer. Editor of Social Reproduction Theory (2017), which collects essays reviving the Wages for Housework analysis in the context of contemporary capitalism, austerity, and feminist strikes.
Italian philosopher and feminist activist who contributed 'From Social Reproduction Feminism to the Women's Strike' to Social Reproduction Theory (2017) and co-wrote Feminism for the 99% (2019).
American philosopher and critical theorist (born 1947). She wrote 'Crisis of Care?' in Social Reproduction Theory (2017) and has written Fortunes of Feminism (2013) and Cannibal Capitalism (2022).

Italian feminist theorist. Author of The Arcane of Reproduction (1981, English 1995), which extends the Wages for Housework argument by analyzing housework and prostitution as two forms of reproductive labor essential to but hidden by capitalism.

aliases: Revolution at Point Zero: Housework, Reproduction, and Feminist Struggle
glossary.explain: Silvia Federici's 2012 essay collection (PM Press) spanning four decades. Reprints Wages for Housework texts and later essays on globalization, reproductive labor, and care crises, introducing the analysis to a new generation.
Bristol-based radical press that published The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972) and, jointly with the Power of Women Collective, Federici's Wages Against Housework (1975).

American feminist writer and activist (1921–2006). Author of The Feminine Mystique (1963), which critiqued the confinement of middle-class women to domesticity and urged entry into paid work. Wages for Housework theorists later argued this doubled women's labor without challenging capitalism's reliance on unpaid housework.

Betty Friedan's 1963 book describing the malaise of middle-class American housewives confined to suburban domesticity. Friedan advocated careers and paid work as liberation; Wages for Housework critiqued this as ignoring that capital requires unpaid domestic labor whether women also work outside the home or not.

The resurgence of feminist activism and theory from the 1960s through the 1980s in the U.S. and Europe. Wages for Housework emerged within the radical wing of second-wave feminism, critiquing liberal feminism's focus on workplace equality while capital continued to rely on unpaid housework.

A second-wave feminist slogan asserting that experiences labeled private—housework, sexuality, childcare, domestic violence—are structured by political power relations. Wages for Housework applied this to argue that the unwaged status of housework is a political decision, not a natural fact.
Canadian chemist and feminist whose 1969 essay 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation' argued that women's unpaid work in the home was a form of production on which the economy relied.
Canadian Marxist who took part in the domestic labour debate with his 1974 article 'The Housewife and Her Labour under Capitalism.'
British economist and feminist who contributed to the domestic labour debate in the 1970s, analyzing women's economic dependency and the relationship between housework and wage labor.

American feminist economist. Author of 'The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism' (1979), arguing that Marxist analysis alone cannot explain women's oppression and that patriarchy and capitalism must be analyzed as dual systems.
Activist who co-founded Black Women for Wages for Housework in 1975 with Wilmette Brown and later became a leading figure in the Global Women's Strike.
German philosopher and economist (1818–1883), author of Capital (1867), whose analysis of labor-power and surplus value the Wages for Housework campaign reinterpreted.
Karl Marx's major work of political economy, first volume published in 1867.
2017 book edited by Tithi Bhattacharya with essays by Lise Vogel, Nancy Fraser, David McNally, Susan Ferguson, Cinzia Arruzza, and others.
aliases: Social Reproduction Theory: Remapping Class, Recentering Oppression

glossary.explain: 2013 book by Nancy Fraser on feminism and capitalism.
2022 book by Nancy Fraser arguing that capitalism consumes the care, nature, and public power on which it depends.

glossary.term: Women, the Unions and Work, or What Is Not to Be Done
glossary.explain: 1972 paper by Selma James, presented at a women's liberation conference in Manchester, which listed wages for housework among its demands.
Icelandic name for the Women's Day Off of 24 October 1975.
Icelandic women's group that proposed the Women's Day Off of 1975.
Icelandic president elected in 1980, the first democratically elected female president in the world.
Trinidadian Marxist writer and activist (1901–1989), with whom Selma James lived in Britain for 25 years.
Black welfare rights leader of the National Welfare Rights Organization who worked with Black Women for Wages for Housework in Houston in 1977.
Black welfare rights leader of the National Welfare Rights Organization who worked with Black Women for Wages for Housework in Houston in 1977.
US organization of welfare recipients, led by Black women including Beulah Sanders and Johnnie Tillmon.
Artist who drew the 1974 poster 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!' for the New York Wages for Housework Committee.
Member of the Toronto Wages for Housework Committee who wrote the text 'Notice to All Governments.'

sections.title: Before Wages for Housework: Marx treating housework as outside production, Friedan-era framing, and second-wave consciousness-raising

blocks.text: Karl Marx's Capital (1867) analyzed how capitalists buy labor-power—the capacity to work—and extract surplus value from its use. Marx noted that labor-power must be reproduced daily (workers need food, rest, shelter) and generationally (new workers must be born and raised). But he treated this reproduction as outside the sphere of capitalist production proper. Women's work in the home—cooking, cleaning, childcare—appeared in Marx's account as part of the worker's consumption, not as labor that produces value. This framing set the terms for a century of Marxist theory that ignored or naturalized housework as a precondition for wage labor rather than as labor itself.

Mid-twentieth-century liberal feminism, exemplified by Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), critiqued the confinement of middle-class American women to suburban domesticity and urged women to seek careers and fulfillment in paid work. Friedan's diagnosis was psychological and individualist: housework was deadening, and liberation meant entering the public world of employment. What this framing missed—and what the Wages for Housework campaign would later emphasize—was that capital benefits whether women do only unpaid housework or whether they do both paid work outside the home and unpaid work inside it. Either way, someone has to cook, clean, and raise children, and capital refuses to pay for most of that labor.

By the late 1960s, the radical wing of second-wave feminism practiced consciousness-raising: small groups of women compared their personal experiences to find shared patterns. The slogan 'the personal is political' named the idea that what looked like private troubles, such as the drudgery of housework or financial dependence on a husband, were shaped by politics and economics. In 1969 the Canadian chemist and feminist Margaret Benston published 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation,' arguing that women's unpaid work in the home was a form of production that the economy relied on. That prepared the ground for the claim the Wages for Housework campaign would make.

sections.title: What Wages for Housework claimed: housework as productive labor that reproduces labor-power, unwaged and thus invisible, essential to capitalist accumulation

blocks.text: The Wages for Housework argument rested on a reinterpretation of Marxist value theory. In classical Marxism, productive labor is labor that produces surplus value for capital—labor performed under capitalist relations of production for a wage. Housework seemed to fall outside: it is unwaged, done in the private home, and its products—meals, clean clothes, cared-for children—are consumed by the family, not sold as commodities. But Wages for Housework theorists argued that this is a mystification. Housework does produce a commodity: labor-power itself. Workers sell their capacity to work to capitalists. That capacity must be produced and reproduced daily—workers need to be fed, clothed, rested—and generationally—children must be born, raised, trained. All of this work is done disproportionately by women, unwaged, in the home.

If housework produces labor-power, then it is productive labor essential to capitalist accumulation. Capital pays workers a wage supposedly sufficient to reproduce labor-power, but in fact that wage covers only the commodities purchased—food, rent, utilities. The labor of transforming those commodities into usable form—cooking the food, cleaning the house, caring for children—is unpaid. It is unwaged labor that capital appropriates. The wage relation thus hides a vast reservoir of exploitation: women's unpaid work subsidizes capital by keeping the wage bill low. Capital does not have to pay for the full cost of reproducing the working class because it externalizes that cost onto women in the home.

The demand for wages was a political strategy, not an economic reform proposal. Wages for Housework organizers did not expect capitalists or the state to start paying women salaries for cooking and cleaning. The demand was intended to make visible what had been naturalized as invisible. Calling housework 'work' and demanding a wage for it denaturalized the ideology that women do domestic labor out of love, maternal instinct, or feminine nature. It named housework as labor and named the wage relation's refusal to pay for it as exploitation. The demand also implied the possibility of refusal: if housework is work, women can refuse to do it, strike against it, or demand that it be socialized and shared rather than privatized and assigned to women.

sections.title: Padua 1972: Dalla Costa, James, Federici, Galtier, and the founding of the International Feminist Collective

blocks.text: The campaign began in 1972. Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici, and Brigitte Galtier are named as its founders, and the International Feminist Collective, formed in Padua, Italy, in 1972, was the organization that launched it. Dalla Costa belonged to Lotta Femminista (Feminist Struggle), an Italian feminist group that grew out of workerism, a current of Italian Marxism that looked for political power in factory workers' everyday refusal of work. James was an American-born writer and organizer who had lived in Britain since 1955, when she moved to marry the Trinidadian Marxist C. L. R. James, and who had written about women and housework since the early 1950s. Federici, born in Parma in 1942, had gone to the United States in 1967 to study philosophy and was living in New York.

In March 1972 James presented a paper, 'Women, the Unions and Work, or What Is Not to Be Done,' to a women's liberation conference in Manchester, England. It listed wages for housework among its demands. Also in 1972, Falling Wall Press in Bristol published The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community, which combined an essay by Dalla Costa with writing by James. This pamphlet is usually treated as the campaign's founding text, and it started what became known as the domestic labour debate.

blocks.alt: Portrait of Selma James, an elderly woman with short white hair, speaking.
blocks.caption: Selma James, co-founder of the International Wages for Housework Campaign, at the Left Forum in New York on 17 March 2012.

blocks.text: The central claim of the Dalla Costa essay is that housework is not a private service outside the economy. Women's unpaid work in the home produces and renews the workers whom employers hire, and because it is unpaid it is hidden, so that it looks like a natural service women give out of love and not like labor. Dalla Costa argued that this made women's struggle in the home part of the wider class struggle, because refusing that work was a way of withdrawing something capital depended on.

sections.title: New York, London, Toronto, Italy: Wages for Housework committees and the Power of Women Collective, Black Women for Wages for Housework, Wages Due Lesbians

blocks.text: After 1972, groups calling for wages for housework formed in several countries. In New York, Federici helped found the Wages for Housework Committee. The first flyer it distributed, in 1973, was titled 'We Can't Afford to Work for Love,' and in 1974 the committee produced a two-colour poster, 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!' The drawing is by Jacquie Ursula Caldwell, and the text, 'Notice to All Governments,' was written by Judy Quinlan of the Toronto committee. Federici and others opened a campaign office in Brooklyn. In Britain, after the Manchester conference, James and several other women formed the Power of Women Collective in London and Bristol, which became the Wages for Housework Campaign in 1975. In 1974, groups calling themselves Salario al Lavoro Domestico appeared in several Italian cities.

blocks.alt: Red and blue 1974 poster showing the Statue of Liberty holding money and a broom, with a list of demands for wages for housework.
blocks.caption: 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice!', a 1974 poster of the New York Wages for Housework Committee. It lists the tasks women want wages for, from every dirty toilet to every cup of coffee and every smile, and ends: 'And if we don't get what we want we will simply refuse to work any longer!' The drawing is by Jacquie Ursula Caldwell.
blocks.credit: New York Wages for Housework Committee, from the collection of Silvia Federici, CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Between 1974 and 1976, three autonomous groups formed inside the campaign in Britain, the United States, and Canada: Wages Due Lesbians, the English Collective of Prostitutes, and Black Women for Wages for Housework. Wages Due Lesbians wanted lesbians included in the wage demand so that it did not go exclusively to 'normal women,' and it asked for the additional physical and emotional work of surviving in a hostile and prejudiced society to be recognized and paid. A 1976 pamphlet from the Toronto group, by Francie Wyland, linked child custody, motherhood, and lesbianism to the wage demand.

Black Women for Wages for Housework was founded in New York in 1975 by Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown. It focused on the situation of Black and third-world women, and it called for reparations for slavery, imperialism, and neo-colonialism. In 1977 the group worked with Beulah Sanders and Johnnie Tillmon, Black women who led the National Welfare Rights Organization, at the first congressionally mandated women's conference in Houston. Together they got the conference to agree that welfare payments should be called a wage.

Not all of these groups lasted. The New York committee that Federici had formed dissolved in 1977, and the Padua group around Dalla Costa left the international campaign and dissolved soon afterward. Dalla Costa has blamed political repression in Italy in the late 1970s for the end of the Italian groups. The London-based campaign and Black Women for Wages for Housework continued, and in 2000 the campaign became more widely known as the Global Women's Strike.

sections.title: Federici's Wages Against Housework (1975): why the demand makes invisible labor visible

blocks.text: Silvia Federici's pamphlet Wages Against Housework was published jointly by the Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press, with a first edition dated April 1975. It is the best-known short statement of the campaign's strategy. The cover carries a list of short lines that became famous: 'They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work. They call it frigidity. We call it absenteeism. Every miscarriage is a work accident.'

blocks.alt: Portrait of Silvia Federici, an older woman with short curly gray hair in a black T-shirt and striped scarf, sitting in front of bookshelves.
blocks.caption: Silvia Federici in an interview in May 2014. Her 1975 pamphlet Wages Against Housework is the campaign's most widely read text.
blocks.credit: Marta Jara, eldiario.es, CC BY-SA 3.0 es

blocks.text: The pamphlet begins by warning against a misreading. Federici says that women often struggle with the idea of wages for housework because they treat it as 'a thing, a lump of money,' instead of 'a political perspective.' If it is only money, she says, it will not seem to change much for women who have other options, such as a professional job or an understanding husband. As a perspective, though, the demand aims to expose and undo the role that capitalism has assigned to women.

The demand is also not an offer to keep doing the work for pay. Federici writes that to demand wages for housework 'does not mean to say that if we are paid we will continue to do it. It means precisely the opposite. To say that we want money for housework is the first step towards refusing to do it, because the demand for a wage makes our work visible, which is the most indispensable condition to begin to struggle against it.' The 'against' in the title therefore points at housework as an unpaid, naturalized duty. The wage demand is the way of naming it as work so that it can be resisted.

She adds that other reforms, such as better social services, will always fall short 'if we do not first establish that our work is work.' In her view, calling housework love is what keeps women doing it without pay and feeling guilty for resenting it.

sections.title: Marxist feminists dispute the strategy: does demanding wages entrench the gendered division of labor or expose capital's dependence on unwaged work?

blocks.text: The campaign set off a long argument among Marxist feminists, the domestic labour debate, which began with The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community. One strand was theoretical. Participants such as Wally Seccombe and Jean Gardiner asked whether housework produces value in Marx's technical sense. If it does not, the wage demand did not fit Marxist categories at all. The debate became intricate, but it had political stakes, because the answer affected whether feminists should organize women as exploited workers in the home.

Others worried that a wage would entrench the gendered division of labor. If the state paid women to do housework, it might become harder to ask men to share it or to move it out of private homes into public services. Wikipedia's summary of the controversy states the usual objection this way: critics argued that the goal should be liberation from housework and from the role of 'housewife,' and that feminists should push for opportunities in paid work and a more equal sharing of unpaid work. Supporters answered that entering paid work does not solve the problem, because many women then work a 'double shift,' with a paid job followed by unpaid work at home. Heidi Hartmann's 1979 essay 'The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism' took a different line from both sides, arguing that Marxist analysis alone could not explain why housework falls to women and that patriarchy has to be analyzed as its own system.

Angela Davis's Women, Race & Class (1981) approached housework from the history of Black women in the United States, for whom, as she showed, the home was never simply a private retreat. Under slavery, Black women's labor, including household labor, was forced for the profit of slaveholders, and after emancipation many worked as domestic servants in white households. In the book's chapter on housework, Davis argued for socializing housework through public services and technology and for women's participation in wage labor, and she was wary that a wage for housework would tie women more tightly to the home. Black Women for Wages for Housework reached a different conclusion from a similar starting point: because Black women did so much paid and unpaid domestic work, they saw the wage demand as a way to claim recognition and compensation.

Federici and James replied that the campaign was not advocating domesticity. The demand was a way of exposing exploitation and starting to refuse it. The disagreement was never settled, but it made the stakes clear: any feminist politics that takes capitalism seriously has to decide what to do about the large amount of unpaid work, done mostly by women, on which everyday life depends.

sections.title: Same years, parallel actions: Iceland's women's day off on 24 October 1975 and the UN International Women's Year conference in Mexico City

blocks.text: In 1975, the year Federici's pamphlet appeared, women in other countries were also putting the value of their work on the public agenda. In Italy, the Triveneto committee for Salario al Lavoro Domestico announced a demonstration in Piazza Ferretto in Mestre, near Venice, for 1 May 1975. The committee covered Venice, Padua, Trentino, and Trieste, which shows how far the Italian groups had spread beyond Padua.

blocks.alt: Pink and blue Italian poster announcing a 1 May 1975 women's demonstration for wages for housework in Mestre.
blocks.caption: Poster for the 1 May 1975 demonstration for 'salario al lavoro domestico' in Piazza Ferretto, Mestre, issued by the Triveneto committee. It lists women's centres in Venice, Padua, Trentino, and Trieste.
blocks.credit: Salario per il lavoro domestico groups, Triveneto, from the archives of Mariarosa Dalla Costa, CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: On 24 October 1975, Icelandic women went on strike for a day. The action was publicized as Women's Day Off (Kvennafrídagurinn), and the idea came from the Redstockings, a women's group, as an event for the United Nations' International Women's Year. Organizers called it a 'day off' because they thought it would persuade more women to join, and because women could be fired for striking but could not be denied a day off. About 90% of Icelandic women took part. They stayed away from paid jobs and did no housework or child-minding. Fish factories closed because so many workers were women, about 25,000 of the country's 220,000 people gathered in central Reykjavik, and fathers who took their children to work made sausages sell out in many shops. The next year, Iceland's parliament passed a law guaranteeing equal rights to women and men, and in 1980 Vigdís Finnbogadóttir was elected the world's first democratically elected female president. The Icelandic strike was not a Wages for Housework action, but it demonstrated in practice what the campaign argued in theory: that daily life stops when women stop doing the unpaid work.

The United Nations declared 1975 International Women's Year and held the first World Conference on Women in Mexico City from 19 June to 2 July 1975. It adopted a World Plan of Action and led to the UN Decade for Women. The conference also showed how divided women's movements were: many delegates from developing countries regarded sexism as a Western concern, and the disagreement over priorities between women in rich and poor countries was one of its main tensions. The international Wages for Housework network later lobbied at UN women's conferences in the 1980s and 1990s on the subject of unwaged work.

sections.title: After the 1970s: the Global Women's Strike from 2000, social reproduction theory in the 2010s, care-work debates, and basic income proposals

blocks.text: The original organizations did not all survive the 1970s, as described above, but the argument kept circulating. Over the 1980s and 1990s, women entered paid work in large numbers without being relieved of housework, which feminists called the 'double shift' or 'second shift.' Wealthier households increasingly hired domestic workers, many of them migrants, to do cleaning, cooking, and childcare, and scholars described 'global care chains' in which women from poorer countries cared for children abroad while others looked after their own children at home.

The international Wages for Housework campaign kept organizing and lobbying. In 1999, after Irish women asked for support for a national strike on International Women's Day, it called for a global women's strike, and on 8 March 2000 women in more than 60 countries took part. The network has been known since then as the Global Women's Strike, coordinated from London, and it now campaigns for what it calls a 'care income' for people who do unpaid caring work.

In 2004, Federici published Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation. The book argues that the European witch hunts of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were part of the violent creation of capitalism, which depended on disciplining women into unpaid reproductive work. It became one of the most widely read feminist books of its generation, and a new edition appeared in 2014.

In the 2010s, a group of Marxist feminists developed these ideas into social reproduction theory. Tithi Bhattacharya edited Social Reproduction Theory: Remapping Class, Recentering Oppression (2017), which includes essays by Nancy Fraser, David McNally, Susan Ferguson, Cinzia Arruzza, and Bhattacharya herself. Fraser's chapter, 'Crisis of Care?', argues that capitalism depends on care work while undermining the conditions that make it possible. Fraser has developed the argument in Fortunes of Feminism (2013) and Cannibal Capitalism (2022).

Some of the wage idea has also reached law and policy. In 2021 a new civil code took effect in China. Article 1088 allows a spouse who has taken on extra duties in raising children, caring for elderly relatives, or assisting the other spouse's work to ask for compensation at divorce. In a 2021 Beijing case, a district court ordered a husband to pay his former wife 50,000 yuan for five years of housework. In India, several state governments began cash transfers to women in the 2020s, of roughly 1,000 to 2,500 rupees a month, and the BBC estimated that about 118 million women in twelve states were receiving them. Whether such payments recognize unpaid work or only compensate for it, and whether they reduce or reinforce the expectation that women do it, is the same question the campaign and its critics argued over in the 1970s.

When you eat a meal someone else cooked, wear clothes someone else washed, or benefit from someone else's care for a child or an elder, do you ask who did that work, whether they were paid, and whose labor subsidizes the economy's claim to efficiency by being naturalized as invisible rather than recognized as essential?
